info.title: Verifying that &kdump; captures a crash dump

abstract.para: After configuring &kdump;, confirm it works by simulating a real kernel crash. Otherwise you only find out &kdump; is misconfigured when an actual crash happens, when it is too late to fix.

warning.title: This test crashes the system
warning.para: Triggering a kernel panic immediately restarts the system, the same as a real crash would. Make sure no important workloads are running and no other users are logged in before you continue.

step.para: Force an emergency sync of cached data to disk, to reduce the chance of data loss from the deliberate crash:
Force an emergency remount of file systems to read-only, to reduce the risk of corruption:
The system panics immediately. &kdump; captures a dump, then the system reboots on its own. This can take a few minutes depending on how much memory needs to be written.
Once the system is back, confirm a dump was captured:
&kdump; creates one directory per captured dump, named after the date and time of the crash (YYYY-MM-DD-HH-MM). Inside it:

example.title: Contents of a captured dump directory
example.screen: -rw------- 1 root root 80731 Sep 10 11:33 dmesg -rw------- 1 root root 309 Sep 10 11:33 README.txt -rw------- 1 root root 67188846 Sep 10 11:33 vmcore

listitem.para: dmesg is the kernel's own ring buffer log at the moment of the crash.
vmcore is the actual memory snapshot. See to read it.
README.txt summarizes the capture itself: kernel version, crash and dump time stamps, dump level, and dump format. Check it first if a capture looks incomplete or was truncated.
